newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia ethnic problems persist after year of peace.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia ethnic problems persist after year of peace.

text.p: Serious mistreatment of minorities in Bosnia is cementing ethnic barriers which peace was meant to destroy and is undermining all efforts to rebuild communal harmony, international agencies said on Wednesday.

The forced eviction of two Moslem families from Croat west Mostar in the last two days forms an ugly backdrop to a London conference hoping to win fresh pledges from local leaders to respect minority rights, a U.N. refugee agency spokesman said.
The two new cases brought the year's total for west Mostar to 69, with an illegal eviction almost every day for the last week, said UNHCR spokesman Kris Janowski.
"This is the most intense wave of evictions from west Mostar since Dayton and it is extremely alarming," he said.

The November 1995 Dayton accords ended Bosnia's 43-month war and were supposed to lead to ethnic harmony through shared government and the return of refugees and displaced people to homes they lost in the fighting.

But almost none of the 250,000 refugees have been able to return to territory controlled by their former foes and minorities have continued to be harassed and expelled by hardliners bent on creating ethnically pure zones.
"The reunifying provisions of Dayton, reunification in terms of ethnic integration, have certainly been very disappointing," Janowski said.
"With regard to minorities, in the opinion of the United Nations, the situation is about as grim as it gets," Alex Ivanko, spokesman for U.N. police monitoring human rights problems, said.
The London conference that opened on Wednesday to review progress in Bosnia after a year of peace is expected to criticise all factions for failing to support refugee returns.
But agencies on the ground see little hope for improvement.
"It is up to the authorities (in the Croat half of the divided southern city of Mostar) to crackdown (on harassment) but they have failed to do it," Janowski said.
"The only way to solve this problem is to pressure the leaders to sort it out but right now they are not sorting it out," Ivanko said.

Officials in London say economic aid may be cut to factions breaking human rights pledges but diplomats in Sarajevo say there is division on the extent to which conditions should be attached to financial help and on the effect of the practice.
NATO's well-armed 50,000-strong peace force, soon to be slimmed to 30,000, says it can do little to help but has been criticised for not taking a tougher stand on refugee issues.

The Bosnian Serb republic has been the most obstructive of the two entities that make up Bosnia, using bombs and armed attacks to dissuade refugees from returning and continuing to force out the few Moslems left in the Serb half of the country.

But the picture is not bright in Bosnia's other half, the Federation, where Moslems and Croats have not overcome the bitterness of their 1993 war and refuse in most cases to allow each other's refugees to return to abandoned homes.
Last week Moslem authorities in the central Bosnian town of Vares evicted the head of the local Croat radio station, despite strong protests from U.N. agencies, Ivanko said.
Some Serb refugees have returned to live in Sarajevo and the northern city of Tuzla where there is a stronger tradition of ethnic tolerance, despite low-level harassment, he added.

Janowski blamed Mostar's problems on criminal gangs who run the city and on Zagreb for pushing Croat refugees to move there. They then buy the homes of freshly evicted Moslems from intermediaries they meet in bars, he said.
